title: Count it all joy (James 1:1–8)
hook: trials produce patience; ask God for wisdom, who gives generously

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Philippians, and your line was I have learned contentment. Did you wait a day before buying something? Day six hundred sixty-nine.

New letter, new voice. Paul wrote long, winding sentences. The letter of James is short and blunt, more like a book of proverbs than an argument. It's written to "the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad", believers living far from home. Tradition says the writer is James, the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem. Churches hear that word brother differently. Protestants often take it plainly, a younger brother. Catholic tradition often speaks of a cousin or close relative, and Orthodox tradition of a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage. Either way, his very first instruction sounds upside down.

In the King James Bible: "My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations." Divers means various, and temptations here means trials, tests of every kind. Fall into, like falling into a pit you didn't see. Count it all joy. Not feel it, count it. It's a decision about how you'll book the thing, not a mood. Why? "Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience." The word for trying means a test that proves what's genuine. And patience here is a strong word: endurance, the strength to keep going. James says trials build that, and then let patience finish its work, so you'll be whole, lacking nothing. And if you're in the middle of a trial and don't know what to do? "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him." Upbraideth not. In James's picture, God doesn't scold the one who asks. No sigh, no eye roll, no you should know this by now. Just generosity. James adds one condition: ask in faith, without wavering, because the one who wavers "is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed." Such a person, he says, is double minded, literally double-souled. Not simply someone with questions. Someone pulled two ways at once, asking God for wisdom while planning not to listen.
screen: `COUNT IT JOY: A DECISION, NOT A MOOD.`
then, large: `LET HIM ASK OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for wisdom. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're facing where you honestly don't know what to do. A decision at work, a relationship, a choice about money or health. Name it plainly. Then imagine bringing it to someone who will never make you feel stupid for asking. If you pray, you can ask God for wisdom about it, simply, in your own words. If you don't, sit with the question openly, as if an answer could come. Notice if one part of you is asking while another part has already decided. The bell holds the time.
Count it all joy. James's first instruction: book your trials as joy, because testing builds endurance, and ask God for wisdom.
Your line: ask for wisdom. Today, ask one person you trust for advice on something real, and actually listen to what they say. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians facing a decision sometimes pray the words of James 1:5, asking God for wisdom, and study groups often read the letter of James as a practical guide to everyday faith.

notes: Authorship: traditionally James the brother of the Lord (Galatians 1:19); some scholars doubt it. The script says 'tradition says'.

Views on 'brother': Protestant (often a son of Mary and Joseph), Catholic (often a cousin or relative) and Orthodox (often a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage). The script compresses Catholic and Orthodox views into 'a cousin or a stepbrother'; confirm wording.
δίψυχος (1:8): its earliest attested use is commonly said to be James; also in the Shepherd of Hermas and 1 Clement. Confirm.
δοκίμιον (1:3) as testing/assaying of metal: confirm gloss.
Practice lightly adapted to ask for wisdom 'if you pray'.
